content: Countries, particularly in sub-Saharan Africa, have integrated and expanded differentiated service delivery (DSD) models into their national HIV treatment policies, especially for adults who are stable on antiretroviral therapy (ART). The concept of stability on ART should be applied universally across all populations, including those on secondand third-line regimens, individuals with controlled comorbidities, children, adolescents, pregnant and breastfeeding women, and key populations. These groups often face challenges in achieving retention in care and viral load suppression, making them particularly suited to benefit from tailored DSD models for HIV treatment. The World Health Organization (WHO) has established criteria to determine whether a person is considered stable on ART. These include: Receiving ART for at least six months. Absence of current illness, excluding well-controlled chronic conditions. Demonstrated understanding of lifelong adherence, supported by adequate counseling. Evidence of treatment success, such as at least one suppressed viral load result within the past six months. If viral load testing is unavailable, alternative indicators include a CD4 count >200 cells/mm³, weight gain, absence of symptoms, and no concurrent infections. For children aged 3–5 years, a CD4 count >350 cells/mm³ is recommended. Updated recommendations emphasize that ART provision should not depend on receiving other services. DSD for HIV treatment aims to separate clinical consultations from other visits, such as ART refills or psychosocial support. Clinical consultations may differ in structure from ART refill visits or psychosocial support sessions. Psychosocial support can be integrated with clinical consultations and ART refill visits or provided separately through community and peer support systems. Multi-month ART refills can be implemented alone or within any of the four DSD categories, offering benefits to both health systems and clients. For children older than two years, multi-month refills are feasible as dosage adjustments become less frequent. DSD models for HIV treatment are categorized into four types: 1. Group models managed by healthcare workers. 2. Group models managed by clients. 3. Individual models based at facilities. 4. Individual models outside facilities. Group models managed by healthcare workers involve people living with HIV who meet at a designated time and location, either at a facility or in the community, facilitated by a healthcare worker (including lay workers). These groups provide peer support, education, and medication distribution. ART adherence clubs are a common example. A South African study involving 3,216 participants showed high retention rates (95% at 12 months, 89% at 24 months) and viral suppression (97% with viral load ≤400 copies/mL). Members of adherence clubs demonstrated better retention and viral suppression compared to those in conventional care. Group models managed by clients involve geographically close individuals who meet at a community location and nominate a member to collect ART for the group on a rotating basis. Examples include community adherence groups and community ART refill groups. Data from sub-Saharan Africa show improved retention, reduced costs, and time savings for clients, as well as peer support benefits. Healthcare workers favor these models for their ability to reduce clinic congestion and workload. Individual models based at facilities, such as fast-track or quick pick-up systems, streamline ART refills by assigning specific times and locations for medication collection without requiring clinical consultations. Evidence shows reduced waiting times, fewer missed appointments, and lower costs for both clients and health systems. These models have demonstrated positive impacts on retention and viral suppression. Individual models outside facilities include fixed community points (e.g., private or community pharmacies), mobile outreach, and home delivery. Fixed community points have shown high retention rates and viral suppression in countries like the Democratic Republic of the Congo, South Africa, Uganda, and Zambia. Home delivery has been studied in Kenya, South Africa, and Uganda, with mixed results on retention and mortality. However, home delivery often reduces costs for both patients and health systems. People-centered care is a cornerstone of effective HIV service delivery. Health systems should invest in practices that improve relationships between patients and healthcare providers, including ongoing training, mentoring, and supportive supervision. HIV programs should prioritize care that respects individual dignity, addresses the needs and preferences of vulnerable populations, and engages patients and families in their care. Addressing stigma and discrimination in healthcare settings is critical to improving access to HIV services, particularly for key populations. Community-based HIV testing and ART initiation outside health facilities are important strategies to enhance access to care. These approaches are particularly relevant in settings where distance, stigma, or other barriers limit access to traditional healthcare facilities.
